pillar_reactions.evidence: Presented as three to four sessions of 30-45 minutes plus a daily five-to-fifteen-minute mobility routine aimed specifically at his balance and tight hamstrings. He confirmed 'Yes' and then asked a precise structural question to check his understanding: 'So you say that the program is approximately 20 to 45 minutes a day. And out of that time, about five to 15 minutes is a mobility type exercise? I just want to make sure I'm understanding the way you're saying it.' Engaged with the mechanics rather than the value. Note his earlier unanswered question — 'I don't know that working with a kettlebell will help with balance, I really don't know' — was never explicitly resolved, only folded into the mobility claim.

The most substantive nutrition exchange in the batch and the only place the prospect visibly engaged with content rather than concept. He volunteered his gluten intolerance and its evidential basis, then challenged the low-carb framing directly — 'I remember I was trying to eat more fruit and somebody was saying, oh no, those are full of carbs... well, they're healthy carbs, aren't they?' — and then connected the eating-window explanation to his own reading: 'I'm really been reading a lot about intermittent fasting... I try not to eat before 10am or after 6pm. Is that what you're talking about?' The rep answered all three well, and the gluten point landed as a genuine match. This pillar was working.

Delivered as teach-a-man-to-fish over six months, video form feedback, chasing messages ('hey, what are you doing, Richard?') and progressive loading. He raised no questions about the mechanism at all; his only interjection during it was a different concern — 'I've never been interested in bulky muscles... I don't want to have a pair of guns' — which the rep handled well. Given that he had just spent ten minutes explaining that prescribed, externally imposed exercise kills his motivation, the accountability pillar was arguably the wrong pitch for him and drew no reaction either way.

anchors.raw: I was of this opinion that this is going to be, you know, like any kind of a membership where it's 30, 40 a month
anchors.note: The anchor that decided the call and the widest gap in the batch — roughly thirty times the quoted price. It exists because nothing framed the price before the call: no setter is named on this file, the lead came in through an application, and his own wife had told him 'you're not going to spend very much'. Contrast the Rudolph call the previous day, where the setter had already given an insight into cost and $6,000 landed as a logistics question rather than a shock.

anchors.raw: I mean, I can get a gym membership. Actually, I've got the YMCA. I can go work out at the YMCA for free. I won't have the guidance. I have an ex-student who's a nutritionist who has guided me off and on when I've had nutritional questions.
anchors.competitor: YMCA membership plus a former student who is a nutritionist
anchors.note: The strongest free alternative in the batch: gym access at zero marginal cost and free professional nutrition advice from someone who owes him a personal debt as his former teacher. He even concedes the one thing missing — 'I won't have the guidance' — which is precisely the gap the offer fills, and it was never picked up.

anchors.raw: I have a dietary plan that I know can get me down to somewhere around 170, 180, with just diet and continuing everything else I'm doing... I did this diet. It starts with a juice cleanse, and then I took out certain foods that my body doesn't react to well, and I dropped right down to 170.
anchors.note: Not a hypothetical alternative — a protocol he has personally executed to a measured result. He restates it as the closing argument: 'I don't need to spend $6,000 to validate that I need to do this. It's just a matter of doing it.' The counter exists in his own testimony, because he then admits he has not restarted it for six months and 'keeps finding excuses'. The rep pressed that hard in Phase 4 and never brought it back when the anchor reappeared at the close.

anchors.raw: in the very beginning, when I told my wife I was having this meeting, she's like, well, you know, you're not going to spend very much
anchors.note: The household budget was pre-framed downward before the call even started, by a spouse who also dismisses his gluten intolerance as being 'in his head'. She is a negative influence on two fronts and was never engaged on either.

anchors.raw: I've got debts and things, and there's no way I can afford 6,000
anchors.note: Debts plus a mortgage that runs another year. Note the timing though: the house is paid off in about twelve months and he is already planning what to do with the freed capacity — a farm, or travel. His capacity to buy changes materially next year, which makes him a legitimate long-nurture rather than a dead lead.

anchors.raw: I know a lot of people that would be able to afford that
anchors.note: He explicitly accepts the price is legitimate for others and never disputes the value — 'It's not that my health isn't worth $6,000.' The objection is capacity and alternatives, not scepticism about worth, which is why discounting would have been the wrong move and holding the price was right.

unmet_demand.want: Guided, personalised coaching at anywhere near $30-100 a month
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Nothing in the range exists. The rep gestured at a community product with standard programmes but never named its price, and the reduced $3,000 tier he did mention was also refused. Even the $200/month self-study tier offered to other prospects in this batch is five times his stated ceiling. This is a genuine hole in the product ladder relative to what an inbound application can attract.

unmet_demand.want: A programme he finds intrinsically enjoyable rather than one that works by external accountability
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He said it as clearly as anyone could — 'if I'm not finding joy in it, I'm not going to do it', and he abandoned a prescribed gym circuit precisely because 'there was no joy'. The offer's central mechanism is accountability, check-ins and chasing messages, which is closer to the thing that failed him than to the thing that works. The rep asserted once that people describe kettlebells as joyful, but never built the case, never connected it to how he trains now (walking through nature, watching sunrises), and never resolved his stated doubt: 'I really don't know if this particular activity is going to fulfill me.' The programme may well suit him; nothing on the call demonstrated it.

unmet_demand.want: Confirmation that kettlebell training addresses balance, which is the deficit that made him fall over
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He asked outright and flagged his own uncertainty — 'I don't know that working with a kettlebell will help with balance as much as, I really don't, in all honesty, I don't really know' — and never received a direct answer. Balance was later swept into a general claim about the mobility routine. He had fallen and injured himself three weeks earlier, so this was the most concrete problem on the table.

unmet_demand.want: Programming safe for a right shoulder with a repaired labrum and rotator cuff
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Both surgeries were disclosed in response to a direct question and then never mentioned again, despite kettlebell training being heavily overhead and pressing. He is 67 and dismissed his own history as resolved, which is exactly when a screening step matters. Third instance in this batch of a disclosed musculoskeletal or medical issue that received no follow-up.
